What experience tells us before we design anything

Three decisions we'd get right before this becomes a final design

These are the three calls we want on record before a single wall gets poured, each one earned from what actually goes wrong on site, not from a textbook.

01 — Technology choice

Build the membrane in once. Don't pay to add it twice.

A conventional ASP or SBR looks cheaper today. But tertiary membrane filtration ahead of discharge is very likely to become a mandatory requirement soon, not an optional upgrade. Retrofitting a membrane stage into a plant that wasn't built for one typically costs close to double what it takes to integrate it from day one. Going with MBR now isn't the premium option, it's the version that never has to be rebuilt.

Conventional now, UF retrofit later
MBR now — built once
02 — Screening

The plant is only as good as what never reaches it.

Every blower, diffuser, pump and membrane downstream depends on debris never getting past the first stage. We'd specify a mechanised, automatic fine screen at the inlet rather than a manual bar screen, so an unattended night shift or a monsoon surge doesn't become the moment something expensive gets damaged.

automatic fine screen
03 — Tank depth

Five metres, not seven.

The tentative plan you'll see on the next page runs the aeration tanks close to seven metres of water depth. Every extra metre adds hydrostatic pressure the diffusers have to push air against, which lowers oxygen transfer efficiency, wears diffuser membranes faster, and pushes the blower selection into a higher-pressure, higher-energy category. Servicing diffusers at that depth is also a genuinely harder maintenance job. Five metres keeps oxygen transfer efficient and diffuser access practical for the life of the plant.

7 m — as drawn
higher blower pressure
5 m — recommended
efficient oxygen transfer

The technical case

Why membrane bioreactor, specifically for a medical campus

Click through each point. These are the reasons this decision is different for an institution training doctors than it would be for a hotel or an apartment complex.

Pathogen and AMR barrier

Medical college wastewater carries a higher load of antibiotic residues and resistant organisms than ordinary domestic sewage. A conventional activated sludge process relies mainly on biological degradation and settling, both of which allow a fraction of resistant cells to pass through in the final effluent. The MBR membrane is a physical barrier below the size of bacteria — it retains that biomass mechanically, independent of how the biology performs on a given day. For a campus that trains doctors, this is the argument that actually matters, not just water clarity.

Footprint

The full treatment building, from bar screen to treated water tank, fits inside an envelope of roughly 36 m by 21.4 m — under 780 sqm — because the membrane replaces the secondary clarifier and lets the biological tanks run at a higher biomass concentration. A conventional ASP sized for the same 1.5 MLD load, with a separate clarifier and larger aeration volume, would need meaningfully more land than your campus has to give.

Reuse quality

MBR permeate is consistently low enough in suspended solids and turbidity to be reused directly for gardens, flushing, or cooling makeup water without a separate tertiary filtration stage — a real operating cost saving over the life of the plant, and it is exactly the treated water tank shown in the drawing that will feed that reuse line.

Odour and neighbours

A properly designed and covered system, with the bar screen and oil and grease chambers kept as sealed open-type units with removable covers per the drawing notes, and controlled aeration through the tank layout, essentially eliminates the odour complaints that come with an overloaded or poorly operated conventional system.

Compliance record

Consistent effluent quality, not just occasional grab-sample compliance, is what protects an institution during a pollution control board inspection or an NABH or NMC review. This is the difference between a system built to pass a spot check and one built to actually run clean every day.

Inside the membrane tank

What is actually happening in MBR Tank 01 and 02

This is a working sketch of the two membrane tanks shown on the drawing, not a decoration. Air scours the membrane surface continuously to keep it from clogging. Suspended solids, floc, and bacteria stay on the feed side. Only clean permeate is drawn through to the treated water tank.

Feed side — mixed liquor, aeration tank 01 & 02
Permeate — to treated water tank

Pore size below 0.4 micron — small enough to mechanically stop bacteria and suspended solids from crossing, regardless of how the biology is performing that day. This is the physical barrier the pathogen and AMR argument on the previous section rests on.

The process, as drawn

Where the water goes, tank by tank

Follow the line. It gets calmer and cleaner as it moves right, the same way the water actually does — from raw inflow on the left to clear, reusable permeate on the right.

Main treatment train — inlet to reuse Side streams — sludge and membrane cleaning

Waste sludge is drawn off from the biological stage into the sludge holding tank for disposal. The CIP tank holds cleaning solution for periodic membrane clean-in-place, keeping permeability stable over the life of the membranes.
